grammar.title: 2A: Present perfect and past simple
grammar.explanation:
The **present perfect** is **have** or **has** + the **past participle**. Use it for past experiences when you don't say when, like a strange customs check or a long layover.

Also use it for recent actions with a present result, often with **just**, **already**, or **yet**. Our boarding has just started, so the aisle is still empty.

The **past simple** is for finished actions when we say, ask, or know when they happened. We missed our connection last Friday because the shuttle was late.

Use **ever** and **never** with the present perfect to ask about life experiences: a crazy transfer, a wrong platform, a lost carry-on.

Never use the present perfect with a past time expression like **yesterday** or **last week**. Don't say "I have seen the itinerary yesterday" — say "I saw the itinerary yesterday."
examples: *I have planned* my itinerary three times this week. (present perfect: experience, no time said)
*She has just finished* packing her carry-on. (just + present perfect = recent action)
*They have never taken* a night shuttle before. (never + present perfect = zero experience)
*Have you ever missed* a connection at a big airport? (ever + present perfect question)
*We have already passed* through customs. (already + present perfect = sooner than expected)
*Our boarding started* at six o'clock this morning. (past simple + past time expression)
*I waited* on the wrong platform yesterday. (past simple + yesterday)
*She transferred* from the bus to the metro last night. (past simple + last night)
*The layover felt* endless, so we drank three coffees. (past simple, finished action)
*Have you booked* the airport shuttle yet? (yet + present perfect question)

practice.q: Why is "I have seen the new platform yesterday" wrong?
practice.a: Never use the present perfect with a past time word like "yesterday". Say "I saw the new platform yesterday."

practice.q: Present perfect or past simple: "She ___ (lose) her carry-on" — no time is given. Which, and why?
practice.a: Present perfect: "She has lost her carry-on." We don't say when, so the experience matters, not the time.
